title: Ravioli al Burro e Salvia
subtitle: Ricotta and spinach ravioli with browned butter and sage
excerpt: Ravioli al burro e salvia is ricotta and spinach filled pasta dressed with browned butter and crisp sage leaves. It is one of the simplest and most satisfying pasta dishes in the Italian canon: the filling is mild, creamy, and faintly nutmeg-scented; the brown butter dressing is rich and nutty. Together they need nothing else.
sourceNotes: Ricotta e spinaci is the classic filling for ravioli, tortelloni, and mezzelune throughout central and northern Italy. Browned butter and sage (burro e salvia) is the canonical pairing and appears in multiple nineteenth-century Italian cookery texts including Artusi (1891), public domain.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked ravioli in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag. Cook from frozen in boiling salted water for 4 to 5 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the filling up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate.

content.text: Ravioli al burro e salvia is the most forgiving stuffed pasta to start with: the filling is simple to make, the flavour is mild enough to forgive slight imperfections in the pasta, and the brown butter dressing takes two minutes. The key technical step is sealing the ravioli properly, with all air pushed out of each parcel before cutting. Air pockets cause them to burst during cooking.

items.prepNote: defrosted, squeezed completely dry, and finely chopped
finely grated, plus more to serve

content.text: Combine {{ricotta}} of drained ricotta with the finely chopped, completely dry {{spinach-frozen}} spinach, {{parmesan}} of Parmesan, {{nutmeg}} of nutmeg, and {{salt-table}} of salt. Mix well. The filling should hold its shape when pressed in a spoon. If wet, drain the ricotta more thoroughly.
Make the pasta and form the ravioli

Mound {{00-flour}} flour on a surface. Make a well and crack in {{eggs}} eggs. Beat the eggs with a fork, gradually drawing in the flour. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap in cling film and rest for 30 minutes.

Roll the pasta in batches to setting 6 on the pasta machine. On a long sheet of pasta, spoon small mounds of filling (about 1 tsp each) at 4 cm intervals along the centre. Dampen the edges and between the mounds lightly with water. Fold the pasta over to cover the filling. Press firmly around each mound to push out air. Cut between the mounds with a sharp knife or pastry wheel. Press the edges again to seal. Place on a floured tray.
Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a boil. Cook the ravioli for 3 minutes until the pasta is just tender and the filling is heated through.

Meanwhile, melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Add {{sage}} sage leaves and cook until the butter turns nut-brown and the sage crisps. Remove from the heat. Lift the ravioli into the pan with a slotted spoon, adding a splash of pasta water. Toss gently. Serve with more Parmesan.

items.cause: Air pockets inside, or the edges were not sealed properly.
items.fix: Press firmly around each mound of filling before cutting, pushing out all the air. Dampen the pasta edges with water and press hard to seal. Do not boil too vigorously -- a rolling simmer is enough.

items.symptom: The filling is wet and runs when cut
items.cause: The ricotta was not drained enough, or the spinach still had water in it.
items.fix: Ricotta from a tub should be drained in a sieve for at least 30 minutes. Frozen spinach must be squeezed until completely dry -- wring it in a clean cloth if needed.

content.text: Ricotta and spinach is the most common pasta filling in Italian cooking. It appears in many regional forms: ravioli in Piedmont and Lombardy, tortelloni in Emilia, mezzelune in the Veneto and Trentino. Browned butter and sage is the classic dressing for this filling. It is one of the oldest pasta sauces in Italy, used since the sixteenth century. The combination is simple on purpose: no tomato, no cream, nothing to hide the filling.
